difficulty.rationale: Small composite dimension/index/projection exercise; several obligations and representation bridge, but exact arbitrary-s projection equality is already a named theorem. No genuinely novel proof search implied.

items.independent_derivation: Let m=2^n and q=2^a, for n,a nonnegative integer qubit counts. The ordered tensor factor signal has q labels s, system has m labels i; each pair indexes one basis vector, giving q*m=2^(n+a) full dimension (both axes). The flattened value f(s,i)=s*m+i uses signal as high-order and system as low-order. For legal indices 0<=s<q, 0<=i<m, f is in [0,q*m), and quotient/remainder by m>0 recover (s,i); hence the convention is bijective. If J_s maps system row i to flattened row f(s,i), (J_s^* U J_s)_{ij}=U_{f(s,i),f(s,j)}. The product-register reindexing V((s,i),(r,j)) is that same entry with f(s,i),f(r,j); restricting both signal labels to an arbitrary fixed s gives V((s,i),(s,j))=U_{f(s,i),f(s,j)} for all i,j. Thus the two descriptions are pointwise the same m-by-m block; n=0 and a=0 also satisfy the identities. The block comparison itself does not need unitarity.

items.independent_derivation: Let e_l,e_r be finite computational-basis kets over C. Component j of e_l is delta(j,l). Thus (Ae_l)_k=sum_j A[k,j] delta(j,l)=A[k,l], and similarly for r. By linearity A(a e_l+b e_r) = a A e_l+b A e_r = a col_l(A)+b col_r(A). Evaluating this vector at any k yields a A[k,l]+b A[k,r]. No orthogonality of different labels, normalization, or unitary assumption is required: if l=r, both formulas reduce to (a+b) times that single column or entry, including a+b=0. The computation of one full output vector requires the two named column functions (or one if the names coincide); evaluating one output coordinate needs at most the two named scalar entries. This concerns the specified input/witness action only, not arbitrary actions, global certificate checks, or asymptotic runtime.

difficulty.rationale: Two obligations (involution plus same-control CNOT reduction), finite guard reasoning. Involution is a one-call imported theorem; reduction still needs the binary guard identity. Not measured difficulty and not a newly discovered reversible algorithm.

items.independent_derivation: On a finite bit string b, let p(b)=(b(c0)=1 and b(c1)=1) and F(b)=X_t(b) if p(b), otherwise b. Assume c0!=t and c1!=t, without any distinctness assumption on c0 and c1. If p is false initially, F leaves b unchanged and remains inactive. If p is true, X_t changes only the target; both control bits are preserved, so p remains true and the second application applies X_t again. X_t^2=id since the target bit is binary and every other coordinate is unchanged. Therefore F(F(b))=b for every b. If c0=c1=c, the predicate b(c)=1 and b(c)=1 reduces to b(c)=1. Thus F is exactly the ordinary controlled-X basis action with c!=t and not necessarily a three-distinct-wire CCX primitive.

items.independent_derivation: Identify the two bits (c,t) with coordinates 0 and 1, and choose the two controls c and t but target c. Call the resulting actual basis action F. Its table is 00->00, 01->01, 10->10, 11->01. In particular 11 and 01 are distinct legal inputs and both map to 01. Consequently F is not injective, cannot be a bijection/involution, and directly F(F(11))=F(01)=01!=11. The earlier proof lost the control0!=target hypothesis: flipping c when c=t=1 also changes a control bit that determined the guard, so the second application is inactive. The other control remains distinct from target. This is a counterexample to omitting that assumption, not a classification of all possible malformed gate definitions.
